title: Minted phUSD from pull() creates a reflexive feedback loop into the sUSDS/phUSD pool — recipient can liquidate debt into protocol BPT backing, imposing loss on NFT holders
rejection_reason: Premise invalid: recipient is a staking module that distributes phUSD to NFT holders over ~1 year, not a rational arbitrageur. MAX_RATIO=50 is the explicit design bound on this economic loop. Finding describes intended protocol mechanics as a bug.
description:
The economic structure set up by the hook + dispatcher is: (1) users pay USDS to mint NFTs; (2) BalancerPoolerV2 wraps USDS into sUSDS and adds it single-sided to the sUSDS/phUSD Balancer pool, receiving BPT; (3) the hook records `ratio%` of dispatched USDS as phUSD debt; (4) recipient pulls debt as freshly-minted phUSD. The NFT-holder position is economically: BPT of sUSDS/phUSD pool collateral, marked-to-market against the pool spot price.

The key unmodelled dynamic: the phUSD that `pull()` mints is fungible with the phUSD on the OTHER side of the sUSDS/phUSD pool the protocol is LPing into. Once recipient has the minted phUSD, it is a one-step arbitrage to dump that phUSD into the sUSDS/phUSD pool (or via the Balancer router) in exchange for sUSDS. Every unit of sUSDS extracted is a direct reduction of the pool reserves that the protocol's BPT has a pro-rata claim on.

Consequence: a `pull()` followed by a phUSD→sUSDS swap on the bound pool literally takes sUSDS from the LP position held by BalancerPoolerV2 and hands it to recipient, net of the swap fee to other LPs. If the protocol is the dominant LP in this pool (expected, since the pool was set up for exactly this purpose), the protocol is essentially both buyer AND seller of phUSD via the Balancer pool — but only one side (the buyer side, carrying sUSDS away) has the minted phUSD backed by nothing, while the seller side (protocol BPT) loses real yield-bearing asset.

This is a reflexive loss that NFT holders cannot see ex-ante: the BPT they notionally back-stop their claim with is systematically drained by every pull() cycle, scaled by how much of the pool's phUSD side is held by the protocol-adjacent liquidity vs external LPs. The larger the protocol's LP share, the more of its own sUSDS it effectively hands to recipient on every pull() + swap.
impact: NFT-holder claim backing is systematically eroded by design, not through a bug but through mechanism composition: the debt hook mints phUSD, recipient liquidates into the same pool that backs claims, extracting sUSDS. The 'ratio' parameter is advertised as a tax on mint throughput, but it is implicitly a tax on the BPT position whenever recipient behaves rationally (i.e. converts phUSD to the more-liquid sUSDS). The hook's design assumes phUSD is worth USDS 1:1 irrespective of pool composition — but the protocol's own BPT is what makes the pool price reach USDS-parity in the first place.
attack_path: Recipient waits until mintDebt is large (many dispatches have accumulated).
Recipient calls pull() — mints debt phUSD to self.
Recipient immediately swaps phUSD → sUSDS on the sUSDS/phUSD Balancer pool (or via the router).
Swap slippage is absorbed by pool LPs proportional to LP share. If protocol BPT holds the majority phUSD-side position, the protocol's sUSDS reserves on its BPT share shrink accordingly.
Recipient now holds sUSDS equivalent (minus swap fee) to the pulled phUSD — realised as real yield-bearing asset extracted from the pool that backs NFT holders.
No protocol-level check prevents or measures this reflexive drain.
recommendation: Rethink the settlement mechanism: `pull()` should not mint free phUSD into a pool the protocol itself is LPing into, because it creates a guaranteed extractive arbitrage against the protocol's own BPT. Viable alternatives: (1) pull() settles debt by transferring sUSDS directly from the dispatcher's BPT redemption, bypassing the pool-mint step entirely; (2) pull() mints phUSD but enforces a same-tx revocation (recipient must prove phUSD is moved off-pool); (3) introduce a debt token that cannot be traded against the sUSDS/phUSD pool. At minimum, the economic relationship between the debt hook and the pool where dispatcher LP sits should be documented as a known-value-leak if the current design is intentional — today the intent is not stated anywhere.
